query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Doping equal-atomic BCC NbMoTaW with a small amount (~5–10 at.%) of a ductility‐promoting element such as Cr will induce local chemical heterogeneity that forms a fine, secondary ductile phase (e.g., FCC or B2) within a dominant BCC matrix. This dual-phase microstructure is expected to enhance room‐temperature ductility and promote defect recombination under irradiation, while preserving the alloy’s high‐temperature yield strength and BCC structural stability.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW with excellent high-temperature mechanical performance but poor room-temperature ductility and unvalidated experimental irradiation tolerance.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled doping of approximately 5–10 at.% Cr into the NbMoTaW alloy composition during synthesis.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing at room temperature and up to 1600 °C; irradiation experiments using helium ion implantation under reactor-relevant energies and fluences.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dual-phase microstructure consisting of a primary BCC matrix with fine, dispersed ductile secondary phase precipitates at grain boundaries or within the grains.
generation.mechanism: The Cr addition promotes local compositional fluctuations that favor the nucleation of a ductile phase without destabilizing the overall BCC structure. This secondary phase enhances plastic deformation at low temperatures and provides diffusion pathways that facilitate defect annihilation under irradiation, thereby combining improved ductility and irradiation tolerance with maintained high-temperature strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to undoped NbMoTaW, the Cr-doped alloy will exhibit increased room-temperature plasticity (higher elongation and reduced brittleness) and reduced irradiation defect accumulation (smaller, less dense helium bubbles) while retaining a high yield strength at elevated temperatures (~1600 °C).
generation.baseline: Undoped equal-atomic single-phase BCC NbMoTaW alloy.
generation.boundary: The expected improvements are projected to occur over the temperature range from room temperature to 1600 °C and under helium ion irradiation conditions typical of reactor-relevant environments.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal concentration of Cr, the exact nature and distribution of the secondary ductile phase, and potential precipitation or embrittlement effects at specific irradiation conditions remain uncertain and subject to experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of alloys: one set of the standard equal-atomic BCC NbMoTaW and a second set doped with 5–10 at.% Cr. Process both sets under identical conditions. Then conduct a series of experiments including mechanical tests at room temperature and at high temperatures (up to 1600 °C), and perform helium ion irradiation under reactor-relevant fluence and energy conditions. Follow up with detailed microstructural characterization (XRD and TEM) to assess phase structure and defect evolution.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile and compressive ductility (e.g., elongation to failure, strain-to-failure)
Yield strength and hardness at elevated temperatures
Phase composition and secondary phase distribution via XRD and TEM
Helium bubble size and density post-irradiation using TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cr-doped NbMoTaW alloy does not show statistically significant enhancements in room-temperature ductility and irradiation defect mitigation (as evidenced by larger ductility metrics and reduced defect accumulation) without a detrimental loss in high-temperature yield strength compared to undoped NbMoTaW, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractIn the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications (e.g. fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. Combining the two approaches above, the authors have recently developed a refractory low-activation HEA based on W-Ta-Cr-V. Its response to loop formation under ion irradiation and He implantation is enhanced compared to previously developed W-based alloys, showing no noticeable dislocation loop formation and smaller He bubbles with no radiation-induced segregation at grain boundaries upon heavy ion irradiation and He implantation, respectively. However, this quaternary RHEA demonstrated Cr- and V-rich precipitates which could be detrimental to mechanical properties in terms of embrittlement. In this study, a design strategy to further improve the overall response of the W-Ta-Cr-V RHEA is introduced and resulted in the development of a quinary RHEA with improved resistance to high-temperature and irradiation environments. Refractory HEAs (RHEAs) stand out among various types of HEAs due to their unparalleled mechanical properties at high temperatures exceeding 800 °C, and even up to 1500 °C in some cases [,], making them viable options for high-temperature structural applications, outperforming typical Ni-based superalloys. Refractory high-entropy alloys, thanks to their high strength at high temperatures, high melting point, and high hardness brought by their resistance to friction and wear properties, may be used in aerospace engines, gas turbines, and the nuclear irradiation field. However, the reported literature has primarily centered on compression deformation investigations. For most RHEAs, due to their room-temperature brittleness, their tensile ductility is commonly negligible []. Therefore, improving the room-temperature plasticity of RHEAs is the premise of its high-temperature application.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have shown promising potential applications in advanced reactors due to the outstanding mechanical properties and irradiation tolerance at elevated temperatures. In this work, the novel low-activation Ti2ZrHfxV0.5Ta0.2 HEAs were designed and prepared to explore high-performance HEAs under irradiation. The microstructures and mechanical properties of the Ti2ZrHfxV0.5Ta0.2 HEAs before and after irradiation were investigated. The results showed that the unirradiated Ti2ZrHfxV0.5Ta0.2 HEAs displayed a single-phase BCC structure. The yield strength of the Ti2ZrHfxV0.5Ta0.2 HEAs increased gradually with the increase of Hf content without decreasing the plasticity at room and elevated temperatures. After irradiation, no obvious radiation-induced segregations or precipitations were found in the transmission electron microscope results of the representative Ti2ZrHfV0.5Ta0.2 HEA. The size and number density of the He bubbles in the Ti2ZrHfV0.5Ta0.2 HEA increased with the improvement of fluence at 1023 K. The preeminent properties (such as high strength [,], good corrosion resistance [,,], fine tribological properties [,], remarkable softening resistance [,], and outstanding irradiation tolerance [,,,], etc.) enhance the application competitiveness of HEAs under extreme environments. Among them, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) [], which are characterized by a high melting point and prepared by methods such as vacuum arc melting, suspension melting, spark plasma sintering [], and wire electric discharge machining [], are expected to play a role in future high-temperature applications []. Compared with conventional alloys, HEAs, especially the body-centered cubic (BCC) structured ones composed of refractory elements, exhibit better irradiation tolerance for the extreme lattice distortions and chemical complexity, such as prominent resistance to hardening [,], suppressed dislocation evolution [,,], low volume swelling rate [,], and reduced radiation-induced segregation [,,], etc. Hence, the HEAs are considered to be a promising candidate for nuclear structural materials [,]

The presence of intermetallic compounds, such as brittle Laves phases, typically reduces the ductility of RHEAs (), prompting extensive efforts to develop single-phase RHEAs for high-temperature applications (, , , , , , ). The equiatomic Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy is one of the most attractive RHEAs, which solidifies as a single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) microstructure with heterogeneous elemental distribution and exhibits excellent high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta has an extremely high compressive yield strength, 1273 MPa at room temperature and 688 MPa at 900°C (). By comparison, conventional high-temperature Ni-base superalloys notably soften above 600°C, with the compressive yield strength dropping to ~200 MPa at 900°C (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta also exhibits impressive tensile ductility, ~14% at room temperature (), and a relatively low brittle-to-ductile transition temperature between −47° and −27°C, comparable to BCC metals and stainless steels for engineering applications (, ).
